Consult Summary:
- Telemedicine consult for an adult with 2–3 days of wheeze and exertional shortness of breath on a background of atopic asthma; clinical impression is an asthma exacerbation, with plan to increase short-acting bronchodilator use via spacer, begin peak flow monitoring, add regular antihistamine, and arrange follow-up in one week with safety-net advice.

History:
- Presenting complaint: Wheezing and feeling short of breath.
- Timeline:
  - Onset: 2–3 days ago.
  - Course: Persistent; limits walking to work; currently comfortable at rest.
  - Prior similar episodes: Had asthma as a child; reports prior similar symptoms in adulthood but cannot recall details.
- Exacerbating/relieving factors:
  - Exertion worsens dyspnea; sometimes difficulty completing sentences during episodes.
  - No home peak flow meter; no spacer.
  - Patient uses salbutamol inhaler intermittently (see PMH/Medications).
  - Potential triggers discussed by clinician: seasonal allergens (pollen) or viral infection.
- Associated symptoms:
  - Dry cough.
  - Reported “feverish,” but measured temperature 37°C.
  - Denies sputum and hemoptysis.
  - Denies chest pain.
  - No nocturnal awakenings.
  - Able to climb stairs; currently feels well at rest.
- Pertinent negatives:
  - No smoking.
  - No known drug allergies.

Past Medical History:
- Asthma (childhood; “quite bad”):
  - Background: Required inhalers; occasional hospital visits; no ICU admissions; occasionally missed school.
  - Adult course: Patient states asthma “stopped” and medication use ceased ~3–4 years ago; later reports ongoing intermittent salbutamol use every few weeks and with exercise (conflict noted).
- Atopy:
  - Hay fever (no current treatment).
  - Eczema (no treatment mentioned).
- Other medical conditions: None reported.

Medications:
- Salbutamol inhaler PRN; patient reports use every few weeks and with exercise (dose/route/frequency not fully documented).
- No other regular medications reported.

Allergies:
- No known drug allergies.

Social History:
- Tobacco: Never smoker.
- Alcohol: ~1 glass of wine every 2–3 days.
- Living situation: Lives with partner.
- Occupation: Engineer.
- Functional impact: Usually walks to work; currently working from home or on sick leave due to dyspnea.

Family History:
- Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
- Vitals: Self-measured temperature 37°C.
- General: Teleconsultation; patient reports feeling well at rest; able to speak during call; can manage stairs.
- No in-person exam performed.

Investigations:
- None performed during this consult.
- Equipment at home: No peak flow meter; no spacer.

Assessment & Plan:
- Issue 1: Acute asthma exacerbation (likely mild to moderate), probable triggers include allergen exposure or viral illness.
  - Assessment: 2–3 days of wheeze, exertional dyspnea, dry cough; atopic history and known asthma; afebrile by measurement; no chest pain; no hemoptysis; no nocturnal symptoms; comfortable at rest but exercise-limited.
  - Plan:
    - Short-acting bronchodilator: Increase salbutamol to 2–4 puffs every 4 hours initially (inhaled; exact dose per device not documented).
    - Spacer: Prescribe spacer; pharmacist to demonstrate use.
    - Peak flow monitoring: Prescribe peak flow meter; record values morning and evening for the next week.
    - Follow-up: Schedule asthma review in ~1 week to assess control, review peak flow diary, and determine need for additional inhaler/other medication.
    - Safety net: Call back urgently if temperature rises, wheeze/shortness of breath worsens, or if difficulty speaking in full sentences persists/worsens.
- Issue 2: Allergic rhinitis/hay fever, possible contributor to bronchospasm.
  - Plan:
    - Begin a regular over-the-counter antihistamine; pharmacist can advise on selection and dosing.
    - Monitor for improvement in upper and lower airway symptoms.
- Issue 3: Possible viral upper respiratory infection precipitating bronchospasm.
  - Plan:
    - Supportive care and monitoring.
    - No antibiotics indicated based on current history.
    - Seek care if new fever develops or respiratory status worsens.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx):
- Asthma exacerbation (High): Atopic history with childhood asthma, ongoing intermittent SABA use, acute wheeze and exertional dyspnea over 2–3 days; no alternative acute cardiopulmonary red flags.
- Viral upper respiratory infection/acute bronchitis with bronchospasm (Moderate): Short duration with dry cough; viral triggers commonly exacerbate asthma; afebrile by measurement and no sputum reduce likelihood of bacterial infection.
- COVID-19 infection precipitating asthma (Medium–Low): Cough and dyspnea could fit; lack of fever by measurement and absence of typical systemic symptoms or known exposure reduce likelihood.

Quality checks:
- Missing but expected elements: Full vital signs (HR, RR, BP, SpO2), objective respiratory exam, baseline/previous peak flow or spirometry, detailed inhaler type/dose/technique, immunization/COVID status, family history, surgical history, allergy specifics (non-drug), pregnancy status if relevant, personalized asthma action plan.
- Conflicts: Patient states stopping asthma medication ~3–4 years ago but also reports ongoing intermittent salbutamol use (conflict noted).
- Transcript quality: Minor communication barriers and intermittent clarity; teleconsult format without physical exam or measured vitals.
